draft.post:
A customer emailed us asking why our moisturiser does not claim SPF 50, unlike the product she used to buy.

An SPF rating on a label relies on a testing standard that assumes an application density of 2 mg per square centimetre. For a face, that is roughly a quarter teaspoon of product. Almost nobody applies that much.

When we measured application amounts in our own usability study, our customers applied closer to a third of that standard density.

If you apply a third of the tested amount, you are not getting the protection listed on the packaging. A 50 on the box does not translate to 50 on your face. In India, SPF testing is also often conducted on a brand's own terms.

I am not saying you should stop buying sunscreen. I am saying the number on the label tells you less than you think.

Next time, ask the brand whether their SPF was tested in vivo, which lab performed the test, and whether they can share the report. If they do not have that documentation, that is useful information.
